name: International Rescue Committee: resettlement, asylum and integration (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the IRC's Resettlement, Asylum and Integration spending in the year to September 2025, U.S. $364.1m and Europe $23.3m (statement of functional expenses), Europe split equally over the six countries the 2025 Annual Report names (Germany, Greece, Italy, Poland, Serbia, the UK).
summary: The International Rescue Committee's Resettlement, Asylum and Integration programmes ($387m in the year to September 2025, 94% in the United States): reception, case management, cash and goods, job placement and other services for about 317,000 refugees, asylum seekers and other newcomers, and immigration legal services for 14,049 clients, unaccompanied children among them. It comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000 (combined range 0.002-0.04): the help is worth its money on the site's log-income scale at newcomers' US consumption, which is many times that of the people overseas aid reaches. About half the result is the legal branch, where help that changes a case's outcome is valued as status or the income of staying instead of being removed, with the risk of being killed after removal. The biggest uncertainties are how many legal outcomes the help changes and how much of the services others would have given anyway; both branches are discounted for missing data.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: People served by Resettlement, Asylum and Integration programmes, 2025

source.title: International Rescue Committee, 2025 Annual Report, Executive Summary
source.quote: 330,896 people served by resettlement, asylum and integration (RAI) programs globally

rows.explainer: Counted by the IRC, the US and Europe together (Europe 88,091; the US about 242,800). The report doesn't say whether '2025' is the fiscal or the calendar year; the counts are taken as the fiscal year of the accounts (October 2024 to September 2025).

rows.label: Newcomers served by immigrant legal-services programmes, 2025

source.title: International Rescue Committee, 2025 Annual Report
source.page: p. 28, RAI U.S., IRC Impact in 2025
source.quote: 14,049 newcomers served by immigrant legal-services programs

rows.explainer: Counted by the IRC (US).

rows.label: Legal clients
rows.explainer: The 14,049 newcomers served by legal programmes; the 2,558 unaccompanied children are taken to be among them (the report prints the two counts side by side without saying the children are extra), so they aren't added.

rows.label: People served by the other services
rows.explainer: Everyone served less the legal clients (most legal clients get other services too; they are counted once, in the legal branch).

rows.label: Household size
rows.explainer: The shared US figure; it only turns the IRC's count of people into households and back (people_reached is the count of people either way).

rows.label: Households reached (people ÷ household size)
rows.explainer: The count of people served, in households.

rows.label: People served by the services to newcomers
rows.explainer: People served, the IRC's count.

rows.label: Cost per person served, both branches, with overhead (US$)
rows.explainer: For reading: about {{row:cost_per_person}} a person. The accounts don't split the line between services and legal work; the result doesn't need the split, since both branches are counted against the whole line's cost.

rows.label: Services: cash, goods and paid help per person served (US$)
rows.explainer: Direct assistance and contributed goods in the accounts ÷ people served: about $270, counted at their cost (rent, furniture, cash).

rows.label: Services: share of people served who start a job through the IRC's employment services in the year
rows.explainer: Judgment 4% (1.5-8%): employment is one of several services; in Europe 459 placements came from 8,040 clients of economic programmes among 88,091 served (0.5% of all served, 2025 Annual Report p. 32); the US programmes run larger job-placement services for new arrivals, whose resettlement help is meant to lead to early self-sufficiency through work.

rows.label: Services: earnings brought forward by a job found with the IRC's help (US$)
rows.explainer: Judgment $8,000 ($3,000-15,000): about three months' earlier start at a newcomer's entry wage of about $2,500-3,000 a month; most would find work anyway, so only the months gained count.

rows.label: Services: value per person served (US$)
rows.explainer: Assistance at its cost, plus earnings brought forward by job placements averaged over everyone served. The time of caseworkers, interpreters and teachers is counted only through what it brings (assistance, jobs, the legal branch), not again at its cost.

rows.label: Consumption per person, United States (Consumer Expenditure Survey)
rows.explainer: The shared US figure.

rows.label: Services: newcomers' consumption per person, as a share of the US average
rows.explainer: Judgment 25% (15-40%): anchored on the lowest-income fifth of US households at 45% of the average per household (@united_states.ce_lowest_quintile_vs_all_2024); newly arrived refugees and asylum seekers live on resettlement funds, low first wages and benefits in their first year, below the lowest fifth.

rows.label: Services: newcomers' consumption per person per year (US$)
rows.explainer: About {{row:baseline_consumption}}.

rows.label: Services: years the income gain counts
rows.explainer: One year by construction: the assistance is spent in the year and the earnings brought forward are counted once.

rows.label: Services: gain in ln(consumption) per person
rows.explainer: The value against a year's consumption.

rows.label: Services: life-satisfaction gain per person-year beyond the money's value
rows.explainer: Zero by construction: the services' good is counted as money and income above; a wellbeing gain on top from the same help would count it twice (domestic-services pitfall). Health care is in dalys_averted_per_person.

rows.label: Services: years the life-satisfaction gain lasts
rows.explainer: Not used while the gain is zero; one year by construction.

rows.label: Services: WELLBYs per person
rows.explainer: Zero.

rows.label: Services: healthy years from health and mental-health care, per person served
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.0005 (0-0.002) healthy years a person: a minority of clients get help enrolling in health insurance, follow-up of refugee health screening and counselling; averaged over everyone served the health gain is small next to the money's value. No count or evaluation of the health services is published.

rows.label: Legal: share of clients defending against removal (asylum or other relief in court)
rows.explainer: Judgment 30% (15-50%): the IRC publishes no split of its legal clients by case type. Its Children's Legal Services clients (2,558, 18% of the 14,049) are in removal proceedings; adult asylum seekers in court add to that, but most of the programmes' clients are served by accredited representatives filing applications outside court (adjustment of status, work permits, family petitions, citizenship, Temporary Protected Status).

rows.label: Legal: in removal cases, how much more often a client with counsel wins relief
rows.explainer: Judgment 30 percentage points (15-45): in the national study of immigration courts, the odds that respondents with counsel obtained relief were five and a half times those without (Eagly & Shafer 2015, University of Pennsylvania Law Review 164:1, abstract); among those who sought relief, about 49% vs 23% for the detained and 63% vs 13% for the never-detained (the American Immigration Council's summary of the same data). The Vera Institute's evaluation of New York's universal representation programme for detained immigrants projected success rising from 4% to 48%. These are observational gaps; the selection in them is in legal_evidence_adj.

rows.label: Legal: for applications outside court, how much more often a client with help succeeds
rows.explainer: Judgment 3 points (1-8): most applicants who qualify would succeed alone or with other help; legal help mostly avoids errors, delays and missed deadlines.

rows.label: Legal: share of clients whose case outcome changes because of the IRC's help
rows.explainer: Removal cases × their gap + applications × theirs: about 11%.

rows.label: Legal: gain in ln(consumption) a year from staying in the destination instead of returning
rows.explainer: Judgment 1.5 (0.8-2.5): a newcomer's consumption in the US (about $8,000-13,000 a person) against the origin's for people like them ($2,000-4,000 in Central America, Venezuela, Haiti and Afghanistan at US prices), ln(13,000 / 3,000) = 1.47.

rows.label: Legal: share of lost cases that end in removal or return
rows.explainer: Judgment 50% (30-80%): many people with a final removal order are never removed (ICE removed 271,484 people in fiscal 2024, while an estimated 1.6 million people with final orders of removal were on its non-detained docket in February 2026, Congressional Research Service IF13208), but enforcement rose sharply in 2025, and some leave on their own after losing; the rest stay without status.

rows.label: Legal: gain in ln(consumption) a year from status, for those who would have stayed without it
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/united_states.json): 0.1 on the log scale, from 0.04 to 0.25, from the 1986 amnesty's wage gains (Kossoudji & Cobb-Clark 2002) plus the work authorisation, benefits and credit status brings.

rows.label: Legal: years the changed outcome lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment 20 years (10-40): protection or a green card is for life, but some would have stayed by other routes later, return or move on.

rows.label: Legal: gain in ln(consumption) per changed case, discounted
rows.explainer: Those who would have been removed gain the US-vs-origin gap; those who would have stayed without status gain status's gap; each year discounted.

rows.label: Legal: risk of being killed after removal, per person removed
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.8% (0.2-3%): homicide rates of 20-40 per 100,000 a year in Honduras, El Salvador and Guatemala (UNODC) over 20 years give 0.4-0.8%, higher for people fleeing a named threat; deportees killed after return are documented (Human Rights Watch 2020, 'Deported to Danger').

rows.label: Deaths averted per person served (legal branch's, over the services' count)
rows.explainer: The legal branch's deaths averted (changed cases × the share who would have been removed × the death risk), spread over the people_reached count so the template's row reads per person; it enters the result only through the legal branch below.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted that are of children under five
rows.explainer: Judgment 2% (0-5%): children are about 40% of the world's forcibly displaced (UNHCR Global Trends), but legal clients are mostly adults and teenagers, and returned adults are the ones targeted.

rows.label: Share of deaths over five at 5-14
rows.explainer: Judgment 10% (5-20%): unaccompanied children, mostly 13-17, are a small share of legal clients.

rows.label: Share of adult deaths at 15-49
rows.explainer: Judgment 90% (80-97%): asylum seekers are mostly young adults.

rows.label: Value of a death averted, by the age mix (units of value)
rows.explainer: The shared value of a death by age band × the life-value slider.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, services
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.7 (0.4-0.9): the assistance is counted at its cost; the jobs brought forward have no trial of the IRC's services (studies of US resettlement agencies find early employment varies with agency and local labour markets, not a controlled effect).

rows.label: Counterfactual, services
rows.explainer: Judgment 50% (30-80%): the federal reception money follows each arrival to whichever of the national agencies takes the case; without the IRC another agency, the state and family would provide much of the help, less well where the IRC is the only office.

rows.label: The IRC's share of all resources behind the services
rows.explainer: Judgment 80% (60-100%): volunteers, sponsor groups and public benefits clients are enrolled in (Convention 2); donated goods are already in the IRC's cost.

rows.label: Attribution share, services
rows.explainer: The shared attribution above.

rows.label: Share of reported reach that gets the service as intended
rows.explainer: Judgment 85% (70-95%), both branches: the January 2025 suspension of refugee admissions and of reception funding cut services mid-case for many clients.

rows.label: Funging and leverage
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.95 (0.8-1.05), both branches: most of the line is paid by federal, state and local grants (the IRC helped allocate $35m in state and local budgets in 2025); a donor's dollar fills gaps the grants leave and may partly replace public money.

rows.label: Missing-data discount, services
rows.explainer: Thin: people are counted, but the jobs brought forward are judged with no evaluation of the IRC's services. Counted less by the shared slider (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: All adjustments, services
rows.formula: svc_evidence_adj * svc_counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * svc_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The branch's adjustments multiplied.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, legal
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.65 (0.4-0.9): the gaps above are observational (represented cases may be stronger to begin with, and counsel picks cases); this is the one place that selection is counted.

rows.label: Counterfactual, legal
rows.explainer: Judgment 70% (50-90%): legal aid is scarce (most people in immigration court have no lawyer); some clients would find pro bono or paid help.

rows.label: The IRC's share of all resources behind the legal outcomes
rows.explainer: Judgment 80% (60-100%): clients' own work on their cases, pro bono partners and the courts.

rows.label: Missing-data discount, legal
rows.explainer: Thin: clients counted, the share whose outcome changes judged. Counted less by the shared slider.

rows.label: All adjustments, legal
rows.formula: legal_evidence_adj * legal_counterfactual_adj * legal_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * legal_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The branch's adjustments multiplied.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment: outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row, weighted by its outcome before adjustments in healthy years (each through its unit's fixed bridge).

rows.label: Counterfactual: outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row, weighted by its outcome before adjustments in healthy years (each through its unit's fixed bridge).

rows.label: Missing-data discount: outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row, weighted by its outcome before adjustments in healthy years (each through its unit's fixed bridge).

rows.label: All adjustments combined: outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row, weighted by its outcome before adjustments in healthy years (each through its unit's fixed bridge).

rows.label: People assisted with family reunification, 2025

source.title: International Rescue Committee, 2025 Annual Report
source.page: p. 29, RAI U.S., IRC Impact in 2025

rows.explainer: Counted by the IRC (US).

rows.label: Reunification: life-satisfaction gain per person reunited (points on 0-10)
rows.explainer: Judgment 1 point (0.3-2): separation from close family is among the largest falls in refugees' life satisfaction in panel surveys of refugees in Germany and Australia; reunion restores part of it.

rows.label: Reunification: years the reunion is brought forward by the IRC's help
rows.explainer: Judgment a year (6 months to 3 years): most families would reunite later through other help or alone; the case work shortens the wait (Faiz's son waited 11 months for a visa after years of applications, 2025 Annual Report p. 31).

rows.label: Reunification: WELLBYs, before adjustments
rows.explainer: A side effect of the services: people reunited × the gain × the years brought forward, discounted. Read at the shared side-effect weight.

rows.label: People served through humanitarian reception programmes in the US, 2025

source.title: International Rescue Committee, 2025 Annual Report
source.page: p. 29, RAI U.S., IRC Impact in 2025
source.quote: 69,818 people served through humanitarian reception programs

rows.explainer: Counted by the IRC: mostly people released at the southern border, given shelter, travel help and information.

rows.label: Humanitarian reception: value of shelter and travel help per person beyond the assistance counted (US$)
rows.explainer: Judgment $100 ($30-300): a few nights' safe shelter, meals and help to reach family elsewhere in the US, at what a bus ticket and cheap lodging cost; their cash and goods are already in assistance_per_person.

rows.label: Humanitarian reception: gain in ln(consumption) per person
rows.explainer: A side effect of the services: the safety value on the site's log-income scale. Read at the shared side-effect weight.

rows.label: Side effect: public money for integration the IRC's advocacy won, as a share of the result
rows.explainer: The IRC's teams influenced the allocation of more than $35 million in state and local budgets for resettlement and integration, going to the IRC and its partners (2025 Annual Report p. 30); the IRC's part is already in this line's spending, so only the partners' part counts: if half went to partners and a fifth of that ($3.5m, about 1% of the line's cost) was moved from other public uses to services worth this model's value per dollar, it adds about 1%. +1% (0 to +3%).

rows.label: Side effect: help from family, sponsors and community the services replace, as a share of the result
rows.explainer: Newcomers with an agency's help lean less on relatives and co-ethnic networks, which would have given part of the same help; the counterfactual counts other agencies, not this. -2% (-5% to 0).

rows.label: Side effects not in the branches, as a share of the modelled result
rows.explainer: The signed side effects above, each estimated against the result; reunification and humanitarian reception are valued in the services branch.

rows.label: Services: units of value, after adjustments
rows.explainer: (People × ln gain + humanitarian reception's safety value, a side effect) × the shared value of ln(consumption).

rows.label: Legal: units of value, after adjustments
rows.formula: (legal_people * legal_outcome_change * legal_ln_gain_per_case * $uov_per_ln_consumption + people_reached * deaths_averted_per_person * value_per_death) * legal_total_adj
rows.explainer: Changed cases × the income gain, plus the deaths averted (deaths_averted_per_person × the count it is spread over) × their value.

rows.label: All units of value, after adjustments
rows.explainer: Both branches.

rows.label: Healthy years from units of value
rows.explainer: The fixed bridge (normalization.md 2.6).

rows.label: WELLBYs, after adjustments
rows.explainer: Reunification's WELLBYs (a side effect), after the services' adjustments but not their counterfactual, since the years brought forward already are the difference the help makes; the services' own life-satisfaction gain is zero (see ls_gain_per_person_year).

rows.label: Healthy years from WELLBYs
rows.explainer: The fixed bridge (normalization.md 2.6).

rows.label: Healthy years from the services' units of value
rows.explainer: The fixed bridge.

rows.label: Healthy years, services, after adjustments
rows.explainer: Income, wellbeing and health of the services.

rows.label: Healthy years, legal, after adjustments
rows.explainer: The fixed bridge.

rows.label: Healthy years, services, before adjustments
rows.explainer: For the outcome-weighted averages.

rows.label: Healthy years, legal, before adjustments
rows.explainer: For the outcome-weighted averages.

rows.label: Healthy years counted directly (health care in the services)
rows.explainer: After the services' adjustments.

rows.label: Healthy years, both branches
rows.explainer: The branches' healthy years (each already adjusted), plus the side effects not in the branches (each read at the shared side-effect weight).

rows.label: Healthy years per dollar
rows.explainer: Outcome ÷ cost.

rows.label: Staff pay as a share of cost
rows.explainer: The line's own personnel share from the accounts (Convention 1): {{row:staff_cost_share}}.

rows.label: Pay gap of staff against comparable jobs
rows.explainer: The shared gap for caseworkers and field staff at nonprofits.

rows.label: Staff's forgone pay (US$)
rows.explainer: What staff give up, counted as their contribution.

rows.label: Your dollar's share of the full cost
rows.explainer: With credit by share of resources, staff's forgone pay counts as part of the cost.

rows.label: Years of healthy life per dollar you give
rows.explainer: The headline.
